hook.line: Vale's mother wants to know what the new accountant is like. Nobody in Bogotá answers with a list of skills: they hand down a verdict in one noun.
hook.es: Es una fiera para los números.

examples.es: Es una fiera para los números.
Es un gallina, no se atreve.
examples.en: He's a chicken, he doesn't dare.

examples.es: Vale es una máquina en la cocina.
examples.en: Vale is a machine in the kitchen.

examples.es: Hernando es un genio para manejar.
examples.en: Hernando is a genius at driving.

rule: English judges a person with an adjective: *she's good with numbers*. Spanish often hands down the verdict as a noun after *ser*: *es una fiera* (a wild animal), *es un lince* (a lynx), *es una máquina*. Keep the little word *un* or *una*. Here's the trap: the noun keeps its own *un* or *una*, whoever you mean. *Vale es un genio*, *Hernando es una fiera*. Only a few insults switch to match a man: *es un gallina*. To say what at, add *para*: *una fiera para los números*. It is warm and informal, and some verdicts sting: *es un gallina* is not a compliment.
smallPrint: Teachers call these evaluative nouns. They describe a person the way an adjective would.

readAndPick.es: Es un gallina, no se atreve.
options: He's a chicken, he doesn't dare.
She's a chicken, she doesn't dare.

readAndPick.es: Eres un genio para los postres.

options: He is a genius at driving.

readAndPick.es: Somos unas máquinas en la cocina.
Mi hermana es un lince para los precios.
options: My sister is razor-sharp with prices.
My brother is razor-sharp with prices.

readAndPick.es: Hernando es una fiera para los números.
options: Hernando is a whiz with numbers.
Hernando's wife is a whiz with numbers.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *un* or *una*: Mi tía es ___ genio para los números. Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.answer: Mi tía es un genio para los números.
yourTurn.why: *Genio* keeps its own *un*, even for your aunt.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *un* or *una*: Hernando es ___ fiera para manejar. Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.answer: Hernando es una fiera para manejar.
yourTurn.why: *Fiera* keeps its own *una*, even for a man.

yourTurn.prompt: Vale is a machine in the kitchen.
yourTurn.answer: Vale es una máquina en la cocina.
accept: Vale es una fiera en la cocina.
yourTurn.why: The verdict is a noun after *es*, and *máquina* comes with *una*.

yourTurn.prompt: She's a chicken, she doesn't dare. (about a woman)
yourTurn.answer: Es una gallina, no se atreve.
accept: Ella es una gallina, no se atreve.

yourTurn.why: *Lince* comes with *un*, and no *muy* is needed: the noun already says it.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about a woman: *Es un gallina, no se atreve.*
yourTurn.answer: Es una gallina, no se atreve.
accept: Ella es una gallina, no se atreve.
yourTurn.why: *Gallina* is one of the few that switch: *un* for a man, *una* for a woman.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about two men: *Mi primo es un genio para manejar.*
yourTurn.answer: Mis primos son unos genios para manejar.
yourTurn.why: Everything goes plural: *mis primos son unos genios*.

yourTurn.prompt: You're an angel, thanks. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: *Ángel* is the verdict, with *un* in front.

pitfalls.wrong: Vale es una genia para los postres.
pitfalls.right: Vale es un genio para los postres.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Genio* keeps its own *un*, even when you mean a woman.

pitfalls.wrong: Ella es fiera para los números.
pitfalls.right: Ella es una fiera para los números.
pitfalls.why: Keep the little word: the noun is the verdict, so it needs *una* in front.

pitfalls.wrong: Hernando es un genio de manejar.
pitfalls.right: Hernando es un genio para manejar.
pitfalls.why: To say what someone is brilliant at, Spanish uses *para*.

personal: Think of someone you know well. Judge them in one noun: *Mi amigo es un genio para...*, or *Mi hermana es una máquina para...*
